summary: Hunger: the want of food felt in the body, and famine, the want of bread in a land. The verb is to be hungry, and its hiphil to make or let hunger, as Yahweh made Israel hunger in the wilderness to teach them that man lives by what comes from his mouth; the adjective is the hungry man, whom the righteous feed and Yahweh fills with good. The noun רָעָב is famine, the heavy famines of Abraham's, Joseph's and Elijah's days, and the famine Yahweh sends with sword and plague on a people who break his covenant, and promises to take away when he gathers Israel to their land. Its constant partner is thirst, and its opposite plenty (שָׂבָע); Ugaritic rġb “be hungry” and Ge'ez rəḫba show the same sense, Arabic raġiba the greedy desire behind it.

words.summary: About a hundred times. Most often famine, a land without bread; less often the hunger a man feels, beside thirst. In the prophets it is one of Yahweh's judgments, with the sword and the plague.

senses.definition: A time when a land or city has no bread: crops fail or a siege cuts off food, and people go elsewhere to buy grain or die. It is said to be “heavy” (כָּבֵד) or “strong” (חָזַק), and to “consume” the land.

evidence.note: “There was רָעָב in all the lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.”
“There was no bread in all the land, for הָרָעָב was very heavy.”
In the siege of Jerusalem “הָרָעָב was strong in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land” (also Jer 52:6).
“Seven years of רָעָב will arise after them, and all the plenty (הַשָּׂבָע) will be forgotten … and הָרָעָב will consume the land.”
Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn “because the famine was heavy in the land”.
A famine in Isaac's days, “besides the first famine that was in the days of Abraham”.
Jacob's sons came to buy grain, “for the famine was in the land of Canaan”.
Elimelech left Bethlehem for Moab because of famine.
Three years of famine in David's days, for the blood of the Gibeonites.
“The famine was strong in Samaria” in the drought of Elijah's days.
In the siege of Samaria a donkey's head sold for eighty pieces of silver.
“Yahweh has called for a famine, and it will come on the land seven years.”
“He called for a famine on the land; he broke every staff of bread.”
Fields and houses mortgaged “to get grain in the famine”.

senses.gloss: famine as judgment, with sword and plague
senses.definition: Famine sent by Yahweh on a people that sins against him, named with the sword and the plague (and wild beasts) as his means of cutting off man and beast.

evidence.note: “A land, when it sins against me … I will break its staff of bread and send רָעָב on it, and cut off from it man and beast.”
“My four evil judgments, sword and רָעָב and evil beast and plague.”
“He who stays in this city will die by the sword, by הָרָעָב and by the plague.”
Of a people that forsook its Rock: “wasted with hunger, devoured by plague”.
Solomon's prayer: “If there is famine in the land, if there is plague …”
The prophets who said “sword and famine shall not be in this land” will perish “by sword and by famine”.
The famine the remnant feared would follow them to Egypt.
“The evil arrows of famine … I will break your staff of bread.”
“The sword is outside, and plague and famine within.”
“Better were those slain by the sword than those slain by hunger.”
The promise reversed: “I will call to the grain and multiply it, and I will lay no famine on you.”
Yahweh's eye is on those who fear him, “to keep them alive in famine”.
“In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword.”

senses.definition: The want of food felt by a person or people, the pain of an empty body; set beside thirst, nakedness and want.

evidence.note: “Bread from heaven you gave them לִרְעָבָם, and water from the rock you brought out for them לִצְמָאָם.”
“You shall serve your enemies בְּרָעָב and in thirst and in nakedness and in want of all things.”
“You have brought us into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly בָּרָעָב”, against eating bread “to the full” in Egypt.
Children “fainting בְּרָעָב at the head of every street”.
“Its honoured men are מְתֵי רָעָב, and its multitude parched with thirst.”
“To give you to die by famine and by thirst.”

senses.definition: A want, sent as judgment, not of bread but of hearing the words of Yahweh.

evidence.note: “I will send רָעָב in the land, not a famine for bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of Yahweh.”
“They shall run to and fro to seek the word of Yahweh, and shall not find it.”

evidence.locator: Gen.41.54, רָעָב → λιμός; 1Ki.18.2 → λιμὸς; Ezk.14.21 → λιμόν; Amo.8.11 → λιμόν; λιμός renders רָעָב ×84

evidence.note: “A great famine over all the land” in the days of Elijah: the famine of 1Ki 18:2.
“A famine came over all Egypt and Canaan”: the famine of Gen 41:54; 42:5.
Power “to kill with sword and with famine and with death and by the beasts of the earth”: the four judgments of Ezk 14:21.
“Famine, or nakedness, or sword”, the want of Deu 28:48.

parallels.note: “Thirst”: hunger and thirst, the two wants of the body.
“Sword”: famine and sword, with plague the triad of judgment in Jeremiah and Ezekiel.
“Plague”: named with famine in judgment and in prayer.

opposites.note: “Plenty”: the seven years of plenty against the seven of famine.
“Bread”: famine is where there is no bread.

words.summary: The man who is hungry, often “the hungry” as a class of the needy, set beside the thirsty, the naked and the poor. The brief's two qal tokens under this key (Isa 9:19; 44:12) are the verb.

senses.definition: Wanting food, with the faintness and emptiness that go with it; the opposite of satisfied (שָׂבֵעַ).

evidence.note: “A satisfied soul tramples honey, but to נֶפֶשׁ רְעֵבָה every bitter thing is sweet.”
“As when הָרָעֵב dreams, and behold, he is eating, and he wakes and his soul is empty.”
“רְעֵבִים, thirsty too, their soul fainted within them.”
“The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness.”
“They know that we are hungry”, in the siege of Samaria.
The oppressed poor “go naked, and hungry they carry the sheaves”.
Of the wicked: “let his strength be hungry”, wasted for want.

senses.definition: The hungry as those in need, to whom the righteous give bread and whom Yahweh fills; to withhold bread from them is wickedness.

evidence.note: The fast Yahweh chooses: “Is it not to share your bread לָרָעֵב, and bring the homeless poor into your house?”
The righteous man “gives his bread לְרָעֵב and covers the naked with a garment” (also Ezk 18:16).
Yahweh “gives bread לָרְעֵבִים”.
“He satisfies the longing soul, and נֶפֶשׁ רְעֵבָה he fills with good.”
Hannah: “Those who were full hire themselves out for bread, and the hungry cease to hunger.”
Eliphaz's charge: “from the hungry you have withheld bread”.
The fool “leaves the soul of the hungry empty”.
“If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat”; quoted at Rom 12:20.

evidence.locator: 1Sa.2.5, רְעֵבִים → πεινῶντες; Psa.107.9 → πεινῶσαν; Psa.146.7 → πεινῶσιν; Isa.58.7 and Ezk.18.7 → πεινῶντι

evidence.note: “He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty”: Hannah's reversal (1Sa 2:5) and Psa 107:9.
“I was hungry and you gave me to eat”: the work of Isa 58:7 and Ezk 18:7.
“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.”

parallels.note: “Thirsty”: the hungry and the thirsty together.
“Naked”: feeding the hungry and covering the naked, the works of the righteous.

words.gloss: be hungry; (hiphil) make hungry, let starve
words.summary: About twenty times. The brief's six tokens with no stem (2Sa 17:29; Isa 8:21; 32:6; Pro 25:21; Job 5:5; 18:12) are the adjective, filed here by spelling.

senses.definition: To want food and feel it: of a man, a people, a land, young lions; set against eating and against thirst.

evidence.note: “My servants shall eat, but you תִּרְעָבוּ; my servants shall drink, but you shall thirst.”
“They shall not יִרְעָבוּ nor thirst, nor heat nor sun strike them”; quoted at Rev 7:16.
“All the land of Egypt וַתִּרְעַב, and the people cried to Pharaoh for bread.”
The smith “is hungry and there is no strength; he drinks no water and is faint.”
“We will go to Egypt, where we shall see no war … and not hunger for bread.”
“If I were hungry I would not tell you, for the world is mine and its fulness.”
The thief who steals “to fill his soul when he is hungry”.
“An idle soul shall hunger.”
“Young lions lack and hunger, but those who seek Yahweh lack no good thing.”
“When he is hungry he will be enraged and curse his king and his God.”
“He snatches on the right and is hungry, and eats on the left and is not satisfied.”

senses.definition: To cause or allow someone to go hungry: Yahweh's humbling of Israel in the wilderness, and what he does not do to the righteous.

evidence.note: “He humbled you וַיַּרְעִבֶךָ and fed you with manna … to make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that comes from the mouth of Yahweh.”
“Yahweh לֹא יַרְעִיב the soul of the righteous, but the craving of the wicked he thrusts away.”

evidence.locator: Gen.41.55, וַתִּרְעַב → ἐπείνασεν; Pro.25.21 → πεινᾷ; Isa.49.10 → πεινάσουσιν; Isa.65.13 → πεινάσετε; πεινάω renders רָעֵב ×9, with further participles and forms

evidence.note: Quotes Pro 25:21: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink.”
Of the multitude out of the great affliction: “they shall hunger no more, nor thirst any more”, after Isa 49:10.
After forty days' fast “he was hungry”, and answered with Deu 8:3 (Mat 4:4).
“I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger.”

parallels.note: “Humble, afflict”: Yahweh humbled Israel and made them hunger.

opposites.note: “Eat”: the servants eat, the rebels hunger.
“Be satisfied”: he is hungry and is not satisfied.

words.summary: Three times: the hunger of Jacob's households in the famine, and “days of famine”. Ugaritic has the same noun, rġbn “hunger”.

senses.definition: The want of food in a household or a time: what grain is carried home to relieve, and the days in which there is no food.

evidence.note: “Go, carry grain for רַעֲבוֹן בָּתֵּיכֶם”, the hunger of your households.
“They shall not be ashamed in the evil time, and in the days of רְעָבוֹן they shall be satisfied (יִשְׂבָּעוּ).”

cognates.note: In the Baal cycle El asks Athirat, “rġb rġbt … hm ġmit”, “are you very hungry … or are you thirsty?”, and offers her food and drink (KTU 1.4:IV:33–35): hunger and thirst as a fixed pair, as in Hebrew. The noun rġbn answers רְעָבוֹן in form. Ugaritic keeps ġ apart from ʿ, so the ע of רעב stands for an older ġ.

evidence.locator: p. 201, §93 Glossary, /r-ġ-b/: rġbt, rġb inf. abs. “to be hungry”; rġbn “hunger”

evidence.note: The fixed pair /r-ġ-b/ “to be hungry” and /ṣ-m-ʾ/ “to be thirsty”, with “to eat” and “to drink”.

cognates.gloss: desire vehemently, greedily, covet; (raġīb) voracious, a great eater, having a capacious belly; (riġġīb) intensely desirous of much eating
cognates.note: Arabic keeps the craving of hunger rather than the want itself: greedy desire, and of a man a great eater with a wide belly. Arabic shows ġ behind ע, as Ugaritic does. Arabic رعب (rʿb, “fear”), tried by sound correspondence, shares no sense.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1110, art. رغب, رَغِبَ (n15969)
evidence.note: “He desired a thing … vehemently, eagerly, greedily, very greedily, with avidity, excessively, or culpably; he coveted a thing, longed for it, or lusted after it.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1111, art. رغب, رَغِيبٌ (n15980)
evidence.note: “Having a capacious inside, or belly … Voracious; a great eater … desirous of much eating: very greedy, or gluttonous.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1111, art. رغب, رِغِّيبٌ (n15983)
evidence.note: “Very, or intensely, or exceedingly, desirous of much eating.”
Relates the Hebrew to Arabic رَغِبَ “to desire”.

cognates.gloss: be hungry; hunger, famine; hungry, famished; (causative) make hungry, let hunger
cognates.note: The same four words as the Hebrew: verb, noun, adjective and causative. The Ge'ez Bible uses the causative at Deu 8:3, as the Hebrew hiphil. Ge'ez writes ḫ where Ugaritic and Arabic have ġ, not the ʿ Ge'ez usually has for an older ġ; the correspondence is irregular, so no sound is recorded from it.

evidence.locator: s.v. ርኅበ (TraCES entry 2213), citing Pro 25:21; Mat 4:2; 5:6
evidence.note: “esurire”; also impersonal ይርኅበኒ “es hungert mich”.
“esurire facere vel sinere, fame premere”.
“esuriens, famelicus, fame enectus”.

evidence.locator: s.v. ረኀብ (TraCES entry 2217), citing Gen 12:10; 41:30; Amo 8:11
evidence.note: “fames”.
rəḫba “be hungry, hunger (for), desire to eat”; ʾarḫaba “let be hungry, cause to be hungry”; rəḫub “hungry, starving, famished”; raḫab “hunger, famine”.

doctrine.statement: Moses told Israel that Yahweh “humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna … to make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that comes from the mouth of Yahweh” (Deu 8:3); the hunger was his doing, and so was the bread from heaven given “for their hunger” (Neh 9:15). Amos foretold a worse want: “not a famine for bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of Yahweh”, when men would run to and fro seeking the word and not find it (Amo 8:11–12). When Jesus had fasted forty days “he was hungry”, and to the tempter's “command these stones to become bread” he answered with Deu 8:3 (Mat 4:2–4). He said, “I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger” (Jhn 6:35), and called blessed those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Mat 5:6). From the verses: hunger is used by God to humble and to teach, and the want that matters most is the want of his word, which Jesus, a man who himself hungered, lived by and gives.

Yahweh “gives bread to the hungry” and “fills the hungry soul with good” (Psa 146:7; 107:9), and Hannah sang that “the hungry cease to hunger” while the full hire themselves out for bread (1Sa 2:5). The same is asked of his people: the fast he chooses is “to share your bread with the hungry” (Isa 58:7, 10); the righteous man “gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked” (Ezk 18:7, 16); withholding bread from the hungry is named as wickedness (Job 22:7; Isa 32:6). It reaches even an enemy: “if he who hates you is hungry, give him bread to eat” (Pro 25:21), which Paul quotes to the believers (Rom 12:20). Mary's song repeats Hannah's, “he has filled the hungry with good things” (Luk 1:53), and Jesus says that at his coming in glory the righteous will be those who fed him when he was hungry, in feeding the least of his brothers (Mat 25:31–40). From the verses: to feed the hungry is to do what Yahweh does, and it is one of the marks by which the righteous are known at the judgment.

Famine is spoken of as Yahweh's sending: “he called for a famine on the land” (Psa 105:16; 2Ki 8:1). Under the covenant it was the portion of an Israel that forsook him, to “serve your enemies in hunger and in thirst” (Deu 28:48; 32:24), and the prophets name it with sword and plague as his judgments on Jerusalem (Jer 14:15; 21:9; Ezk 5:16; 14:13, 21); Solomon asked that Israel, when famine came for their sin, might pray toward the house and be heard (1Ki 8:37–39). Yet the promise is that when Yahweh takes Israel from the nations and brings them into their own land and cleanses them, “I will call to the grain and multiply it, and lay no famine on you … that you may never again bear the reproach of famine among the nations” (Ezk 36:24–30), and they will “no more be consumed with famine in the land” (Ezk 34:29). Of those whom he gathers it is said, “they shall not hunger nor thirst” (Isa 49:10), which Revelation repeats of the redeemed (Rev 7:16). From the verses: famine in the land followed Israel's breaking of the covenant, and its end is promised in the land itself, when Yahweh regathers and cleanses his people.

note: Drafted 2026-11-19. Root key רעב; no existing entry used it, and no BDB key under it (t.di.aa–t.di.ad) was assigned elsewhere. All four keys are assigned here. Shared tokens: the verb's six tokens with no stem (2Sa 17:29; Isa 8:21; 32:6; Pro 25:21; Job 5:5; 18:12) are the adjective, counted under both keys; the adjective's two qal tokens (Isa 9:19; 44:12) are the verb. Isa 44:12 גַּם־רָעֵב could be read as either; it is cited under the verb. No personal names are formed from the root (none in TIPNR). No Biblical Aramaic word; the brief finds no Peshitta word of the root. Ge'ez ḫ for an older ġ is irregular (Ge'ez usually has ʿ); Ugaritic and Arabic both show ġ. Leads not followed: the Proto-Semitic list's Aramaic RʿB “hungry” (ARM028719), not found in Jastrow's Aramaic or SEDRA, so not recorded; the Akkadian “be hungry” verb (berû) is another root and is not recorded; Ugaritic in DULAT (not vendored); Dillmann's printed columns for the Ge'ez (cited by TraCES entry). Leslau's page is as TraCES records it, not checked in the printed book. Open questions: (1) whether Arabic raġiba “desire greedily” is the same root as the Hebrew or a parallel development from the craving of hunger (marked cognate on the strength of the shared ġ and of riġġīb “desirous of much eating”); (2) whether the figurative “famine of hearing” (Amo 8:11) is worth its own sense or belongs under famine-judgment; (3) the doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review.
